MilliMirror: 3D Printed Reflecting Surface for Millimeter-Wave Coverage Expansion

a fully passive metasurface, which can reshape and resteer mmWave beams to anomalous directions to illuminate the coverage blind spots
Kun Qian  ·  Lulu Yao  ·  Xinyu Zhang  ·  Tse Nga Ng

What it is

The paper's story: where it is used, its core idea and the real system demo.
Real-world use

A printed surface on a wall carries a 5G beam indoors

Imagine a meeting room served by a 60 GHz access point, whose beam a body can block: such rooms are where a printed surface could help.

the surface, seen close

It shows A corner of the surface, seen close: thousands of tiny plastic blocks, each with metal under it.

How to read it Each block's height is set when it is printed; together they aim the reflection.

the surface, turning the beam

It shows MilliMirror on its wall, seen close: the base station's beam comes in and its own beam goes out to the window.

How to read it The gold cone and line are the beam from the base station; the pale ones are the beam it sends to the user.

the phone in hand

It shows The user's phone, seen close: indoors, behind the wall, it gets only the control channel.

How to read it The window beside this one shows the data rate the phone gets.

the receiver's data rate

It shows The indoor receiver's data rate in the paper's outdoor-to-indoor test (60 GHz 802.11ad radios), without and with the surface.

How to read it Without the surface only the 23 Mbps control channel was left; with it the link averaged 770 Mbps.

Motivation

A blocked line of sight leaves millimetre-wave blind spots

  1. 1signals from the outdoor base station cannot reach the indoor user equipment
  2. 2the beam direction is confined by the poses of reflectors
  3. 3the coordination between an active metasurface and the transceivers is still an open problem
where each way sends the beam

It shows Where each earlier way sends the beam: a plate mirrors, a smart surface needs power, a 10 × 10 cm² PCB array costs $200.

How to read it The blind spot is marked; a way works only if its beam reaches it without power or a large cost.

State of the art

Steering a reflection needed power, sync or costly boards

  1. 1Several systems assume a wireline control channel between the smart surfaces and the Tx/Rx
  2. 2existing RF metasurface elements have complex electromagnetic artifacts such as mutual coupling
  3. 3MilliMirror is fabricated using commodity 3D printers
earlier ways, by cost and steering

It shows Earlier ways to fill a blind spot, placed by what they need and where they can send the beam.

How to read it Farther right means passive and cheap, higher means the beam can go any way, and MilliMirror aims at the top right.

Background

Four key terms

Blind spot01

mmWave radios bear a fundamental coverage limitation

A wall or a body blocks the beam.

Metasurface02

RF metasurfaces are artificial surface structures

Tiny elements that reshape a passing wave.

MBDC03

a thick dielectric cuboid on top and a thin metallic layer on the bottom

A metal-backed dielectric cuboid; its height sets its phase.

Beam pattern04

we represent the objective beam pattern by specifying the direction and width

The main lobe is the beam; side lobes leak.

Core idea

Each block's height sets a phase; together they aim the reflection

  1. 1the MBDC to act as a phase shifter with respect to the incident signal
  2. 2the metasurface can form different reflection beam patterns
  3. 3MilliMirror is endowed with the capability of adjusting the reflection signal power to any direction
phase shift against thickness

It shows One block's reflection phase against its thickness: a full 360° over about 1.5 mm, so thickness sets phase.

How to read it Thickness across, phase down; the line is the model, the dots the paper's full-wave simulation (Fig. 2b).

where the reflection goes

It shows The surface's reflection against angle: its beam points where it was designed to, far from the mirror angle.

How to read it Angle across (0° is straight out), strength up in dBsm; the dashed line marks the mirror direction.

the blocks, seen close

It shows A corner of the surface's back, seen close: each step is one block's height.

How to read it Copper is the metal on each block's back, drawn thicker than it is; a taller block delays the wave more.

A printed surface keeps a strong beam out to about 70°

it can reflect mmWave signals towards anomalous directions that do not comply with the Snell’s laws

  2. The printed surface sends its beam where it is designed to
  3. Its design angle sweeps from 10° to 80°
  4. Each colour is one block's height
  5. Its main lobe holds within 4 dB up to about 70°

Challenge 1 · pattern synthesis

Standard searches over thousands of phases converge slowly

they converge slowly and are very likely to end up with poor solutions in a huge searching space like MilliMirror

these algorithms essentially need to search the solutions in randomized manner

  1. New: 4,096 blocks, each phase a free choice
  2. Two standard searches try phase after phase
  3. Fourier iteration (IFT) settles fast but uneven; particle swarm (PSO) stalls
  4. The pattern they reach still misses the target
PSO steps, capped –
PSO time –
PSO main lobe –
PSO side lobe, median –
search error

It shows How each standard search's error changes: IFT, the iterative Fourier transform, settles at once; PSO, particle swarm optimization, barely moves.

How to read it One line a search; lower is less error, as a share of its first, from 1 to 0.8 here; both axes log.

target, patterns

It shows The objective in the u-v plane and in angles, beside IFT's and PSO's patterns: IFT leaves dark gaps, PSO stays weak.

How to read it Bright is strong; u-v is the plane the searches work in; each angle map is ψ across from straight out, ξ up.

Solution 1 · Closed-form synthesis

Differentiable pattern synthesis

we redesign an objective function, which is differentiable with a closed-form derivativeThe new search matches how each element's wave lines up with its neighbours' (the autocorrelation) to the same for the wanted pattern. That alone fixes the pattern's power, and the wanted level comes from the power the surface must send out.

each error term is only related to a few phase shifts with an order of 2In the old error, each term mixes all the phases, raised up to the fourth power. Here each term depends on only a few phases, to the second power (the paper's “order of 2”), so its slope has a short formula, and Newton's method can follow it down.

  1. New: the autocorrelation search sets the phases
  2. Its error falls far below IFT's and PSO's
  3. Its pattern fills the box most evenly
  4. In Table 1 it was the slowest
  5. Your turn Try each search and compare

Challenge 2 · phase only

Phase-only elements leave nulls inside the main lobe

the MBDCs can only modulate the phase, not magnitude, of incident signals, which inevitably results in nulls in the reflected main lobe

minimizing the side lobe level results in nulls in the main lobe region

  1. The target: one flat, even lobe
  2. The 2-D search leaves nulls in it, ringed
  3. A null is a spot the beam misses
  4. The curve shows how uneven the lobe is
Nulls in main lobe –
Main-lobe spread (std. dev.) –
Main lobe level –
target and result

It shows The target beside the 2-D autocorrelation result: its main lobe still has nulls, ringed, where the reflection drops sharply.

How to read it Bright is strong reflection over ψ across and ξ up; the dashed box is the main lobe; rings mark points 10 dB under its mean.

main-lobe levels

It shows Each search's main-lobe levels, as in Fig. 5(g): the 2-D search's long tail on the left is its nulls; the 1-D decomposition has none.

How to read it For each level across, the line gives the share of main-lobe points at or under it; steep is even; dotted: the objective.

Solution 2 · Two 1‑D syntheses

Decomposition into two 1‑D syntheses

For objective patterns with a single main beam, we propose to find a suboptimal solution without nulls

the extension of the main beam only introduces a minor decrease of the MLLTo split the pattern in two, its main lobe is first widened to a rectangle in the u-v plane. MLL is the main lobe level. Our simulation: the 1-D design's is 0.1 dB under the 2-D search's; the paper says only “minor”.

  1. New: two 1-D searches, one per side
  2. Each cuboid adds its row's and column's phase
  3. A flat main lobe: no nulls, no long tail
  4. Your turn Switch 1-D and 2-D; compare the nulls
Nulls in main lobe –
Main-lobe spread (std. dev.) –
Main lobe level –

Challenge 3 · beam squint

Off its design frequency, the beam drifts from its target

the desired phase shifts deviate from the model over a wider bandwidth

it shifts away at edge frequencies of the working band

  1. New: the frequency sweeps 57–71 GHz
  2. At 64 GHz the pencil beam hits 45°
  3. At the band's edges it swings off the target
  4. The larger the surface, the worse the drift

Solution 3 · wideband model

One main lobe for the whole band

we set the main lobe region as the union of the main lobe regions of all frequencies in the working bandA block is at most half a wavelength thick, so its own phase changes little from 57 to 71 GHz (most errors under 20°). Only where each frequency sees 45° moves: one lobe over all those places keeps 45° in the beam.

  1. New: a block's own phase barely changes
  2. In û, v̂, each frequency's 45° sits apartû and v̂ add the incoming and outgoing directions and multiply them by the surface's size in wavelengths. There the blocks' phases do not depend on the wavelength; only the place where each frequency's 45° falls moves.
  3. One lobe takes in every frequency's 45°
  4. So 45° stays in the beam, though weaker
  5. Field test: 1540 Mbps or more on every channel
  6. Your turn Wideband off and on; move the frequency

Challenge 4 · fabrication

The ideal model is not yet a part a printer can make

it is not straightforward to turn the ideal MilliMirror model into a fabricatable metasurface

most the off-the-shelf 3D printing materials only specify ε at very low frequencies

  1. Each block's thickness sets its phase
  2. The thicknesses come in steps of 0.1 mm
  3. Its dielectric constant ε at 60 GHz is unknown
  4. Each error moves the phase off its target
Largest phase error, 64 × 64 paper about 14.5° per 0.1 mm–
Main lobe, fan beam –
ε tried (made for 2.5) –
a row of blocks, cut open

It shows Eight blocks cut open: each block's thickness sets the phase it gives, so a printed thickness off its target moves the phase.

How to read it Grey: the plastic blocks over their metal; above each, its target phase dashed, the phase it gives solid, and the gap between them marked.

phase against thickness

It shows The phase a block gives at each thickness: the printer's steps and a wrong ε move each block's phase off its target.

How to read it Thin line: the ε assumed; thick: the print's own; dots: the 0.1 mm steps; rings: the paper's simulation; short bar: one block's error.

Solution 4 · 3-D print + metal

PA 12 blocks on a plated copper back

The measurement confirms ε = 2.55 around the 60 GHz bandMost printing materials list ε only at very low frequencies. Designed for ε = 2.5, the paper's simulated 4 × 4 cm² beam lost under 1 dB at ε up to 3.5; measuring ε makes that smaller still.

  1. New: HP PA 12, printed by Multi Jet Fusion
  2. Blocks from δt = 0.4 mm, in 0.1 mm stepsA printed part needs a least thickness to be strong: 0.4 mm for HP PA 12. Thicker blocks raise the specular side lobe in the paper's simulation, so the paper keeps δt at 0.4 mm.
  3. Then 10 nm Cr, 300 nm Cu, plated to 15 µm
  4. 15 µm: over 50 skin depths, so no wave passes
  5. No dielectric: the paper finds a strong specular lobe
  6. Your turn Dielectric off and on; then raise δt
Specular, 60.48 GHz –
Main lobe, 60.48 GHz –
Specular, 57 GHz –
Cost, 10 × 10 cm² PCB array $200$15.3

Check the Paper · 2 of 3

Ablation study

Question What does each part of the design add at the receiver?The Rx stands 10 m from the surface at the beam's centre, 45°, the Tx 30° off the normal (our choice, so the incident phase counts and both stand in view). Each part is switched off on the beam the paper uses for it.

You change
MilliMirror's parts, one off at a time

Why it matters Each part guards the link.The incident phase aims the beam. The even power share sets its level. Two 1-D designs remove holes. The band-wide design keeps gain at 45° over the band, at a lower level.

  1. 1Your turn Make it in 2-D.One 2-D design leaves holes, called nulls, in the beam; two 1-D designs do not. With them off, the 2-D search can take three ways (Fig. 5(c–e)). The paper's autocorrelation comes closest to the target. The iterative Fourier transform (IFT) is fast but uneven. Particle swarm optimization (PSO) stalls.
  2. 2Your turn Use one frequency.On Fig. 9's pencil beam over 57 to 71 GHz. A design for 64 GHz alone squints off 45° at the band's edges; the band-wide one keeps gain there, at a lower level.
  3. 3Your turn Drop the incident phase.The Tx stands 30° off the normal, so the wave reaches each element at another phase. A design that ignores this sends the beam elsewhere.
  4. 4Your turn Use a rule of thumb.The paper spreads all reflected power evenly over the beam. A rule of thumb asks for a main lobe 20 dB over the side lobes instead (our margin).
More controls
2-D method, used with the 1-D designs off
Test beam
Main lobe, worst frequency –
Weakest point in the beam –
Mirror-direction side lobe –
RSS at the Rx, 10 m –
All on: RSS at the Rx –

What you saw RSS: the strength at the Rx, the ambient −68 dBm added. Our closed form, like the paper's own phase model, cannot see the full-wave mismatch that makes vacuum grooves fail.the decomposition method eliminates the nulls the absolute MLL will be inevitably reduced compared with the single carrier case The term represents the phase delay introduced by different propagation distances determination of the power delta relies on heuristics This further signifies the need of using MBDC as the unit element in MilliMirror

dB lost without each part

reflection pattern

the reflector, where the Rx stands, and the curved metal's shape

Generalization study

Question Where does a printed reflector stop steering the beam well?The paper simulates beams turned 10° to 80° and surfaces 2 to 8 cm wide (Fig. 6). It measures one band, samples up to 16 cm, the Rx 2.3 to 10 m out. Here each goes further. We look from just behind the surface, its back toward us.

You change
angle, size, band, where the Rx is

Why it matters Users stand far off its face.Each element reflects less as the beam leans away from its face. A bigger surface wins back level, and at a higher band the same surface holds more elements.

AngleSent backSizeBand
  1. 1Your turn Turn the beam past the paper's 80°.A 4 cm surface (our size: Fig. 6(c) gives none) aims a pencil beam at this angle, and the Rx follows it. A flat metal plane of the same size reflects only like a mirror.

Metal plane here –

What you saw Our element reflects with the cosine of its angle, fitted to Fig. 6(c) (assumed). Past 80° the paper has no point.the effective reflection FoV of the MBDC should be around 140° (±70°) at 4 dB tolerance

  1. 1Your turn Move the Tx past the paper's 80°.The 4 cm surface (our size) sends the wave back to the Tx, as in Fig. 6(d); the Rx stands beside the Tx. A plain mirror would send it the other way.

Mirror direction –

What you saw Sending back loses twice: the wave comes in and goes out at a slant. Our mirror-direction lobe comes from the design alone; the paper's full-wave test also finds the surface's own mirror reflection.Given the 4 dB tolerance, the effective FoV of MilliMirror should be around 100° (±50°)

  1. 1Your turn Grow the surface past the paper's 16 cm.The beam aimed 45° off the normal, 20° wide one way and 10° the other, as in Fig. 6(a). Twice the side is four times the elements.
  2. 2Your turn Widen the beam past the paper's 32°.As in Fig. 6(b): the same power spread over a beam twice as wide gives half the level, 3 dB less.

What you saw “All power in the beam” is the paper's objective level: the reflected power shared evenly over the beam. A real pattern loses some of it to side lobes.The MLL steps up by around 3 dB as the surface area doubles

  1. 1Your turn Pick another band for an 8 cm surface.Elements a quarter wavelength wide at each band (assumed). At 140 GHz an 8 cm surface holds 150 × 150 of them.

  2. 2Your turn Drag the Rx farther out.The field test's Rx is 10 m out; the paper's case studies put it 2.3 to 8.3 m out. The strength falls as the square of the Rx's distance.
  3. 3Your turn Turn the Rx away from the surface.Turn it by its ring in the scene, or here. Its one antenna sees less than 120° (§7.3): turned more than 60° away, it misses the surface.

Go Beyond the Paper · 2 of 3

Physical conditions

Question Which real-world flaw costs the link the most?Each tab changes one thing the paper fixes: the place, the material, the printing, the metal. The Tx and Rx stay 10 m from the surface, the Rx at the beam's centre. We look from just behind the surface; the Tx stands off to the right.

You change
the place, the material, the printing, the metal

Why it matters Real prints and sites are never ideal.A site's own reflections shrink the surface's gain. A wrong ε or a coarse step bends each phase a little; many elements share each error, so the beam keeps its shape.

SiteMaterialPrintingMetal
  1. 1Your turn Pick another place to test.Each place has its own reflections without the surface, the paper's measured medians (Fig. 22). The 10 cm pencil sample adds its own path.
    Place
  2. 2Your turn Set the mount straight, at 0°.The mount starts turned 1.1°, the roadside 0.2° more for its uneven ground: our assumption, as the paper names such errors (§8) and gives none. The 1° pencil beam moves about twice as far as the turn.
Gain over the place alone –
Beam moved off 45° –

What you saw With the mount turned as the places had it (assumed), each of our dots sits in its box, the roadside lowest, as §8 says. Straight, the pencil beam lands on the Rx, and ours reads 6 to 9 dB over the paper's medians.accurate measurement must be conducted to reduce the relative location and orientation error of MilliMirror The link achieves the highest gain in the parking lot and lawn The gain in roadside is lower mainly due to the uneven ground of the road the RSS in indoor scenarios is higher than in outdoor scenarios The gain in roadside is lower mainly due to the uneven ground of the road

  1. 1Your turn Set the material's real ε to 3.5.The thicknesses stay those made for ε = 2.55, the paper's measured value. The paper guesses 2.5 to 3.5 for printing materials (§5.1).
Main lobe, 8 cm fan –
Largest phase error –

What you saw Both are drawn as the change from the ε designed for: ours on the 8 cm field fan, the paper's on a 4 cm pencil designed for 2.5 (Fig. 10(a)). Only the trend compares.the MLL of the beam decreases slightly as the error of ε increases

  1. 1Your turn Coarsen the thickness step to 0.3 mm.The paper rounds each thickness to 0.1 mm (§5.1). Each cuboid's phase is then off by up to half a step.
  2. 2Your turn Thicken every cuboid's base to 1.4 mm.The printing material needs 0.4 mm at least (§5.1). A thicker base gives the same phases at the design frequency, but drifts more off it.

What you saw The paper gives no formula for its 14.5°. Our model reads it as 2k·Δt, the free-space round trip of 0.1 mm at 60 GHz, which gives the same number. The paper puts the growing side lobe down to a full-wave mismatch our closed form does not have.the maximum thickness error is no more than 0.1 mm, translating to a maximum phase error of about 14.5° the SLL at the specular reflection direction dramatically increases with thicker dielectric cuboids

  1. 1Your turn Thin the copper to 0.1 µm.The paper plates 15 µm of copper (§5.2). At 60 GHz the wave reaches only about 266 nm into it, the skin depth.

Optimal array setup design

Question How does each added 8 × 8 cm module change the link?A large surface can be spliced from small printed modules (Fig. 11(e)). Here each module carries its slice of one design, so in place they act as one surface.

You change
how many modules there are, and where each sits
  1. 1Your turn PressTwo modules side by side make 16 × 8 cm², the size of the paper's second sample (Fig. 15). Twice the area puts twice the power into the same beam.
  2. 2Your turn PressFour modules make 16 × 16 cm², the size of the paper's third sample, four times the area of one.
  3. 3Your turn Drag a module a little off its place.Off its place, a module's waves travel a different distance to the Rx, so they no longer add in step with the others.
  4. 4Your turn PressBack to one module: 8 × 8 cm², the size of the paper's first sample, which reads −61 dBm at 10 m (Fig. 15).
